9	## 🚀 Project Structure
10	
11	Inside of your Astro project, you'll see the following folders and files:
12	
13	```text
14	/
15	├── public/
16	├── src/
17	│   └── pages/
18	│       └── index.astro
19	└── package.json
20	```
21	
22	Astro looks for `.astro` or `.md` files in the `src/pages/` directory. Each page is exposed as a route based on its file name.
23	
24	There's nothing special about `src/components/`, but that's where we like to put any Astro/React/Vue/Svelte/Preact components.
25	
26	Any static assets, like images, can be placed in the `public/` directory.
27	
28	## 🧞 Commands
29	
30	All commands are run from the root of the project, from a terminal:
31	
32	| Command                   | Action                                           |
33	| :------------------------ | :----------------------------------------------- |
34	| `npm install`             | Installs dependencies                            |
35	| `npm run dev`             | Starts local dev server at `localhost:4321`      |
36	| `npm run build`           | Build your production site to `./dist/`          |
37	| `npm run preview`         | Preview your build locally, before deploying     |
38	| `npm run astro ...`       | Run CLI commands like `astro add`, `astro check` |
39	| `npm run astro -- --help` | Get help using the Astro CLI                     |
40

---

# Personality Rewrite Plan: Jose Lopez Personal Site

## Diagnosis of the Current State

After reading every source file, here is what makes the current site feel like a LinkedIn profile rather than a person:

- **Hero.astro** opens with "AI Engineer. Data Scientist. Builder of intelligent systems." and a generic gradient circle with initials "JL" instead of a real photo. It reads like a conference badge.
- **About.astro** is career chronology: "over two decades of experience," "My journey started in systems engineering back in 1999," and every paragraph leads with an institution (Edinburgh, BCP).
- **Work.astro** has three highlight cards that are credential-shaped ("AI & ML at BCP," "Edinburgh-Trained," "25+ Years in Tech") plus a certifications list. Pure resume.
- **Interests.astro** is labeled "Beyond work" but three of its four cards are still professional: "Artificial Intelligence," "Continuous Learning," "Languages & Culture." Photography gets a single card with one sentence.
- **Nav.astro** uses corporate labels: About / Work / Interests / Contact.
- The color palette (#1a1a2e primary, #e94560 accent) and typography (Inter) are clean and modern. The visual quality is solid. The problem is entirely in the content and the structural priority given to credentials over personality.

---

## 1. New Section Architecture and Order

**Current:** Nav, Hero, About, Work, Interests, Contact, Footer

**New:** Nav, Hero, Photography, Places, Story, Projects, Contact, Footer

The structural principle: lead with the personal, reveal the professional later. A visitor should first encounter Jose the photographer and traveler, then discover he also builds AI systems at Peru's largest bank. That reversal is what turns a resume page into a personal site.

The current **Interests** section gets dissolved entirely. Photography becomes its own visual centerpiece. Places absorbs the geographic/cultural thread. The remaining interests (AI curiosity, languages, learning) weave into the Story narrative.

---

## 2. Section-by-Section Design

### 2a. Nav (`src/components/Nav.astro`)

The current links array at line 2-7 defines the site structure:

```javascript
const links = [
  { href: '#about', label: 'About' },
  { href: '#work', label: 'Work' },
  { href: '#interests', label: 'Interests' },
  { href: '#contact', label: 'Contact' },
];
```

Replace with informal labels that match the new sections:

```javascript
const links = [
  { href: '#photos', label: 'Photos' },
  { href: '#places', label: 'Places' },
  { href: '#story', label: 'Story' },
  { href: '#projects', label: 'Projects' },
  { href: '#contact', label: 'Say Hi' },
];
```

"Story" instead of "About." "Say Hi" instead of "Contact." These small label changes signal tone immediately. The rest of the Nav component (fixed positioning, backdrop blur, mobile menu logic) stays exactly as-is.

---

### 2b. Hero (`src/components/Hero.astro`)

**What changes:** Everything except the HTML structure pattern.

Currently the hero has a gradient circle with "JL" initials (lines 8-9), the title "Jose Lopez," a tagline, a credential line, and two CTA buttons. Every element needs to shift.

**Replace the JL circle with a real photograph.** This is the single highest-impact change on the entire site. The gradient circle at line 8 (`w-32 h-32 mx-auto rounded-full bg-gradient-to-br from-accent to-accent-light`) should become an actual `<img>` tag with a photo of Jose, or the entire hero could use a full-width background image from Jose's photography (a Lima cityscape, a travel shot, something visually striking).

**Rewrite the tagline.** Current (line 15): "AI Engineer. Data Scientist. Builder of intelligent systems." New approach: lead with the personal, let professional context arrive naturally.

Example new hero copy:
- Name: "Jose Lopez" (keep)
- Tagline: "I photograph the world, build things with AI, and collect stories from the places I've been."
- Location line: "Based in Lima, Peru." (strip Edinburgh and BCP from the hero entirely)
- CTA buttons: "See my photos" (goes to #photos) and "More about me" (goes to #story)

**Why this works:** A visitor landing on this page immediately understands Jose as a multidimensional person. The AI credentials appear later in Story and Projects where they have context and depth instead of being a cold opener.

---

### 2c. Photography -- NEW (`src/components/Photography.astro`)

**This component does not exist yet. It is the most important addition.**

Photography is currently a single card in Interests.astro (line 19: "Capturing moments and perspectives through the lens. Follow my visual journey on Instagram."). In the new site, it becomes the first content section and the visual heart of the page.

**Structure:**
- Section id: `photos`
- A short first-person intro: one or two sentences about why Jose photographs, in conversational tone. Not "Photography & Visual Stories" but something like "I started carrying a camera everywhere a few years ago. Now I can't stop."
- A responsive image grid: 6-9 photographs in a clean grid layout
- Each image with optional hover overlay showing location and/or a short caption
- A link to Instagram at the bottom for the full collection

**Technical approach for the grid:**

Use Tailwind CSS grid. The simplest approach that looks professional:

```
grid grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3 gap-4
```

Each image uses a consistent aspect ratio (`aspect-[4/3]` or `aspect-square`) with `object-cover` to maintain visual uniformity. This avoids the complexity of true CSS masonry while looking clean.

For image data, use a frontmatter array:

```javascript
const photos = [
  { src: '/images/photos/photo-1.jpg', alt: 'Description', location: 'Lima, Peru' },
  { src: '/images/photos/photo-2.jpg', alt: 'Description', location: 'Edinburgh, Scotland' },
  // 6-9 entries
];
```

**Image optimization considerations:**
- Use `loading="lazy"` on all images below the fold
- Size images to max 1200px wide for the grid
- Consider Astro's built-in `<Image />` component from `astro:assets` for automatic WebP conversion and responsive srcsets, which would require moving images to `src/assets/` instead of `public/images/`
- Add placeholder background colors or aspect-ratio containers so the page doesn't layout-shift while images load

---

### 2d. Places -- NEW (`src/components/Places.astro`)

**This component does not exist yet.**

The current site scatters geographic references across About and Interests: Lima is mentioned as a location line in the hero, Edinburgh is a credential in About, and "Languages & Culture" is an interest card. The new Places section collects all of this into a personal geography — not a career timeline, but a collection of meaningful locations.

**Structure:**
- Section id: `places`
- Heading: "Places That Shaped Me" or "Where I've Been"
- 3-4 place cards, each with: a photograph, the place name, and a short personal sentence (not a credential)
- Layout: responsive grid, `sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3` or a horizontal scroll on mobile

**Example place entries:**

```javascript
const places = [
  {
    name: 'Lima, Peru',
    image: '/images/places/lima.jpg',
    note: 'Home. The city where the Pacific meets the desert and where I keep coming back to.',
  },
  {
    name: 'Edinburgh, Scotland',
    image: '/images/places/edinburgh.jpg',
    note: 'Where I studied AI and discovered that the best ideas come from long walks in the rain.',
  },
  {
    name: 'A third meaningful place',
    image: '/images/places/third.jpg',
    note: 'A personal connection — travel, family, a formative experience.',
  },
];
```

**Key tone shift:** The current About.astro line 18 says "I studied at **The University of Edinburgh**, one of the world's leading institutions for AI research." The new Places card for Edinburgh would say something warmer and more specific — the university is implied, not headlined.

---

### 2e. Story (replaces About) -- `src/components/About.astro` becomes `src/components/Story.astro`

**What changes:** The file is renamed (or rewritten in place with a new section id). All four paragraphs of copy are replaced. The section id changes from `about` to `story`.

**Current tone problem:** Every paragraph in About.astro leads with a credential or institution. Line 13: "I'm an AI specialist and machine learning engineer with over two decades of experience." Line 18: "I studied at **The University of Edinburgh**." Line 23: "Today I work at **Banco de Credito BCP**, Peru's largest bank." Line 28: "I speak English, Spanish, and some French."

**New tone:** First-person narrative that leads with curiosity and personality. Professional details are woven in rather than headlined.

**Example rewrite:**

> I've been curious about how things work since I was a kid -- taking apart electronics, writing my first programs, trying to understand systems. That curiosity led me from Lima to Edinburgh, from engineering to data science to AI.

> These days I work at BCP, Peru's largest bank, where I get to build AI systems that actually help people. But this site isn't my resume -- it's more like a window into the things I care about.

> When I'm not training models, I'm usually behind a camera, practicing my French, or planning where to go next.

**Structural changes:**
- Could add a side-by-side layout: text on the left, a casual photo of Jose on the right (not a headshot, something candid)
- Could include a small "quick facts" element: current city, languages spoken, favorite camera, what he's reading/watching. This adds personality without more prose.
- The section should be shorter than the current About. Three short paragraphs instead of four long ones.

---

### 2f. Projects (replaces Work) -- `src/components/Work.astro` becomes `src/components/Projects.astro`

**What changes:** The certifications list (lines 2-9) is removed entirely. The highlight cards (lines 11-27) are rewritten from credential-shaped to project-shaped. The section id changes from `work` to `projects`.

**Current problems:**
- The three current highlights are not projects — they are credentials wearing project clothing: "AI & ML at BCP," "Edinburgh-Trained," "25+ Years in Tech." None of these describe something Jose built.
- The certifications list (6 entries, lines 2-9) belongs on LinkedIn, not a personal site.
- The tags on each card are resume keywords: "NLP, LLMs, MLOps, Python."

**New approach:** Describe actual things Jose has built or is building. Focus on what the project does and what was interesting about it, with a personal angle.

**Example rewritten card:**

```javascript
const projects = [
  {
    title: 'AI systems at BCP',
    description: 'I build machine learning tools at Peru\'s largest bank — fraud detection, customer insights, NLP systems that help real people. The challenge isn\'t building the model, it\'s making it work in the messy real world.',
    link: null, // or a GitHub/demo link if available
  },
  {
    title: 'Open source & experiments',
    description: 'Side projects and experiments — the stuff I build because I\'m curious, not because someone asked me to.',
    link: 'https://github.com/aifriend',
  },
];
```

Remove the tags or replace them with simpler, less keyword-stuffed labels. If certifications must be mentioned somewhere, a single line at the bottom of the section ("I keep learning: recent courses from DeepLearning.AI, Edinburgh, and more") with no detailed list.

---

### 2g. Contact (`src/components/Contact.astro`)

**Copy rewrite only.** The structure (four social links in rounded-xl bordered cards + footer) works fine.

**Current heading:** "Let's connect" (generic)
**New heading:** "Say Hi" (matches nav label)

**Current intro (line 13):** "Whether it's about AI, a project idea, or just a good conversation — I'd love to hear from you."
**New intro:** Something warmer and more specific. Example: "I love meeting new people. Whether you want to talk about AI, photography, travel, or something I haven't thought of yet — drop me a line. Best way to reach me: email. Best way to see what I'm up to: Instagram."

**Consider reordering the social links** to put Instagram higher (it's the photography/personal channel) and LinkedIn lower (it's the professional channel, and this site is personal-first).

**Footer (line 69-73):** Currently "Built with Astro." Consider something with more personality: "Made with curiosity in Lima, Peru" or "Built by Jose, powered by Astro and too much coffee."

---

### 2h. Interests.astro -- DELETE

This component gets absorbed into the new sections:
- "Artificial Intelligence" interest card content → woven into Story prose
- "Continuous Learning" interest card content → woven into Story prose
- "Languages & Culture" interest card content → detail in Story + implied by Places
- "Photography & Visual Stories" → becomes the Photography section

The file `src/components/Interests.astro` should be deleted and its import removed from `index.astro`.

---

## 3. Tone and Voice Guide

**Voice:** First person, warm, specific, slightly self-deprecating. Like a friend giving you a tour of their apartment.

**Rules for all copy:**
- Always "I" never third-person references to "Jose Lopez"
- Lead with personal details, then professional
- Use specific details over generic claims: "learning French on Duolingo at midnight" is better than "multilingual professional"
- **Avoid:** "passionate about," "leveraging," "cutting-edge," "solutions," "driving impact," "thought leader"
- **Use:** "curious about," "I built," "I love," "what gets me excited," "I can't stop"
- Shorter sentences. More white space.
- Every section should pass the "would a friend actually say this?" test

---

## 4. Complete File Change Manifest

### New files to create:
1. **`src/components/Photography.astro`** -- Image grid section, new centerpiece
2. **`src/components/Places.astro`** -- Place cards section
3. **`public/images/`** directory tree: `photos/`, `places/`, and a hero image

### Files to heavily rewrite (new copy, possible rename):
4. **`src/components/Hero.astro`** -- Real photo replacing JL circle, personal tagline, new CTAs
5. **`src/components/About.astro`** -- Rename to `Story.astro`, full narrative rewrite, section id `about` becomes `story`
6. **`src/components/Work.astro`** -- Rename to `Projects.astro`, remove certifications, rewrite as personal project stories, section id `work` becomes `projects`
7. **`src/components/Nav.astro`** -- New link labels and href targets
8. **`src/components/Contact.astro`** -- Copy rewrite for warmer tone, footer personality

### Files to delete:
9. **`src/components/Interests.astro`** -- Content absorbed into Photography, Places, and Story

### Files to update:
10. **`src/pages/index.astro`** -- New component imports (Photography, Places, Story, Projects), remove Interests import, new render order
11. **`src/layouts/Base.astro`** -- Update default title from "Jose Lopez -- AI Engineer & Builder" to something personal like "Jose Lopez -- Photos, Projects & Stories from Lima" and update the meta description
12. **`src/styles/global.css`** -- Potentially minor adjustments (the existing palette works; changing copy and adding photos will transform the feel more than a color change would)

---

## 5. Implementation Sequence

**Phase 1 -- Infrastructure**
1. Create the `public/images/photos/` and `public/images/places/` directories
2. Add placeholder images (solid color or low-res placeholders that Jose replaces later with real photographs)
3. Update `src/pages/index.astro` with the new component order and imports

**Phase 2 -- New sections**
4. Create `src/components/Photography.astro` with image grid
5. Create `src/components/Places.astro` with place cards

**Phase 3 -- Rewrites**
6. Rewrite `Hero.astro` with new copy, real photo, CTAs
7. Create `src/components/Story.astro` (rewrite of About) with full narrative
8. Create `src/components/Projects.astro` (rewrite of Work) without certifications
9. Rewrite `Nav.astro` with new labels
10. Rewrite `Contact.astro` with warmer copy

**Phase 4 -- Cleanup**
11. Delete `src/components/Interests.astro` and its import
12. Delete old `About.astro` and `Work.astro` if creating new files rather than renaming
13. Update `Base.astro` title and meta description
14. Test all anchor links with new section ids
15. Test responsive behavior across breakpoints
16. Verify image lazy loading and performance

---

## 6. Anticipated Challenges

**Image dependency.** The Photography and Places sections require actual photographs to deliver their impact. The implementation should use well-sized placeholder containers (with `aspect-[4/3]` and background colors) so the layout works before real images are added, and Jose can drop in his photos incrementally.

**Page weight.** Adding 10-15 photographs to a previously text-only page will significantly increase load time. Mitigation: use Astro's `<Image />` component from `astro:assets` for automatic optimization, lazy-load everything below the hero, and keep grid images at a max width of 1200px.

**Masonry vs uniform grid.** True masonry layout is complex in pure CSS. Recommendation: start with a uniform grid using consistent aspect ratios (`aspect-[4/3]`) and `object-cover`. This looks professional and avoids layout complexity. Iterate to masonry later only if the photo selection demands mixed aspect ratios.

**Section id changes.** Changing `#about` to `#story` and `#work` to `#projects` will break any existing external links or bookmarks. For a personal site this is low risk, but worth noting.

**Content tone consistency.** The biggest risk is half-committing to the tone shift — rewriting some sections in warm first-person while leaving traces of corporate language. Every piece of copy should be reviewed as a whole after the individual section rewrites.

---

## 7. index.astro Final Target Structure

```astro
---
import Base from '../layouts/Base.astro';
import Nav from '../components/Nav.astro';
import Hero from '../components/Hero.astro';
import Photography from '../components/Photography.astro';
import Places from '../components/Places.astro';
import Story from '../components/Story.astro';
import Projects from '../components/Projects.astro';
import Contact from '../components/Contact.astro';
---

<Base>
  <Nav />
  <main>
    <Hero />
    <Photography />
    <Places />
    <Story />
    <Projects />
    <Contact />
  </main>
</Base>
```

1	# Astro Starter Kit: Minimal
2	
3	```sh
4	npm create astro@latest -- --template minimal
5	```
6	
7	> 🧑‍🚀 **Seasoned astronaut?** Delete this file. Have fun!
8	
9	## 🚀 Project Structure
10	
11	Inside of your Astro project, you'll see the following folders and files:
12	
13	```text
14	/
15	├── public/
16	├── src/
17	│   └── pages/
18	│       └── index.astro
19	└── package.json
20	```
21	
22	Astro looks for `.astro` or `.md` files in the `src/pages/` directory. Each page is exposed as a route based on its file name.
23	
24	There's nothing special about `src/components/`, but that's where we like to put any Astro/React/Vue/Svelte/Preact components.
25	
26	Any static assets, like images, can be placed in the `public/` directory.
27	
28	## 🧞 Commands
29	
30	All commands are run from the root of the project, from a terminal:
31	
32	| Command                   | Action                                           |
33	| :------------------------ | :----------------------------------------------- |
34	| `npm install`             | Installs dependencies                            |
35	| `npm run dev`             | Starts local dev server at `localhost:4321`      |
36	| `npm run build`           | Build your production site to `./dist/`          |
37	| `npm run preview`         | Preview your build locally, before deploying     |
38	| `npm run astro ...`       | Run CLI commands like `astro add`, `astro check` |
39	| `npm run astro -- --help` | Get help using the Astro CLI                     |
40	
41	## 👀 Want to learn more?
42	
43	Feel free to check [our documentation](https://docs.astro.build) or jump into our [Discord server](https://astro.build/chat).

```md
# Personality Rewrite Plan: Jose Lopez Personal Site

## Overview

Transform a credential-heavy LinkedIn-style portfolio into a warm, personal showcase that leads with who Jose is — photographer, traveler, curious person — and lets the professional story support rather than dominate.

---

## 1. New Section Architecture & Order

### Current order:
Nav → Hero → About → Work → Interests → Contact → Footer

### New order:
Nav → Hero → Photography → Places → Story → Projects → Contact → Footer

**Rationale:** The current site opens with credentials and buries the personal. The new order flips that — the visitor first sees Jose the person (a striking photo, his photography, the places that shaped him), and only then discovers his professional depth. This is how personal sites with real personality work: they invite you in with what someone loves, then reward your curiosity with substance.

---

## 2. Section-by-Section Design

### 2a. Nav — file: `src/components/Nav.astro`

**Current:** JL logo, links to About/Work/Interests/Contact
**New:** Jose logo, links to Photos/Places/Story/Projects/Say Hi

The nav labels themselves should feel personal and informal. "Story" instead of "About." "Say Hi" instead of "Contact." "Photos" instead of some corporate section name.

\```
const links = [
  { href: '#photos', label: 'Photos' },
  { href: '#places', label: 'Places' },
  { href: '#story', label: 'Story' },
  { href: '#projects', label: 'Projects' },
  { href: '#contact', label: 'Say Hi' },
];
\```

### 2b. Hero — file: `src/components/Hero.astro`

**Current tone:** "AI Engineer. Data Scientist. Builder of intelligent systems." + "Lima, Peru · Edinburgh alumni · Currently at BCP"

This reads like a conference badge. The new hero should feel like meeting someone at a dinner party.

**New approach:**
- Full-width or large background photo (one of Jose's own photographs — a Lima cityscape, a travel shot, something visually striking)
- Name as the focal point, but the tagline is personal-first
- First-person, conversational

**Example new copy:**
\```
Jose Lopez

I photograph the world, build things with AI,
and collect stories from the places I've been.

Based in Lima, Peru.
\```

The hero CTA buttons shift from "Get to know me" / "Say hello" to something warmer:
\```
"See my photos" → #photos
"More about me" → #story
\```

**Component changes:**
- Replace the JL circle avatar with an actual photo (either a headshot or a full-width background image)
- The gradient circle is generic; a real photo immediately makes the site feel human
- Add a `public/images/` directory for hero image and photography assets
- Consider a subtle parallax or fade-in effect on the hero image

### 2c. Photography (NEW) — file: `src/components/Photography.astro`

**This section does not exist yet.** It is the most important addition.

Photography is currently a single bullet point in the Interests section. In the new site, it becomes a visual centerpiece — the first content section after the hero.

**Design:**
- Section heading: "Through My Lens" or simply "Photos"
- A short intro line in first person: "I started carrying a camera everywhere a few years ago. Now I can't stop."
- A responsive image grid (masonry-style or uniform grid) showcasing 6-9 of Jose's best photographs
- Each image could have a subtle hover overlay showing location/caption
- A link to Instagram for more: "Follow the full journey on Instagram"

**Technical approach:**
- Create `src/components/Photography.astro`
- Images stored in `public/images/photos/` (or use Astro's `src/assets/` for optimized images)
- Grid layout using Tailwind CSS grid or flexbox masonry pattern
- Consider a lightbox interaction (could use a small client-side script or keep it simple with links)
- Data structure:
\```javascript
const photos = [
  { src: '/images/photos/lima-sunset.jpg', alt: 'Sunset over Lima coastline', location: 'Lima, Peru' },
  { src: '/images/photos/edinburgh-old-town.jpg', alt: 'Edinburgh Old Town', location: 'Edinburgh, Scotland' },
  // ... more photos
];
\```

**Grid layout options (Tailwind):**
- Simple uniform: `grid grid-cols-2 md:grid-cols-3 gap-4`
- Masonry-like: alternating tall/wide images using `grid-rows` and `row-span`
- Featured + grid: one large hero photo + smaller grid below

### 2d. Places (NEW) — file: `src/components/Places.astro`

**This section does not exist yet.**

Jose's journey from Lima to Edinburgh and through various experiences is currently told as career chronology. The new "Places" section reframes geography as personal narrative.

**Design:**
- Section heading: "Places That Shaped Me" or "Where I've Been"
- A visual layout with 3-4 place cards, each with:
  - A photograph from that place
  - The place name
  - A short personal sentence about what it means to Jose (not "I studied at Edinburgh" but "Edinburgh taught me to think slowly in a city that moves fast")
- This is NOT a timeline. It's a collection of meaningful places.

**Example entries:**
\```javascript
const places = [
  {
    name: 'Lima, Peru',
    image: '/images/places/lima.jpg',
    note: 'Home. The city where the Pacific meets the desert, where I grew up, and where I keep coming back to.',
  },
  {
    name: 'Edinburgh, Scotland',
    image: '/images/places/edinburgh.jpg',
    note: 'Where I studied AI at one of the best universities in the world — and discovered that the best ideas come from long walks in the rain.',
  },
  {
    name: 'A third meaningful place',
    image: '/images/places/third.jpg',
    note: 'Personal connection to this place...',
  },
];
\```

**Technical approach:**
- Create `src/components/Places.astro`
- Horizontal scrolling cards on mobile, grid on desktop
- Each card: image top, place name, personal note
- Could use `grid sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3 gap-6`

### 2e. Story (replaces About) — file: `src/components/About.astro` → rename/rewrite to `src/components/Story.astro`

**Current tone:** Third-person credentials ("I'm an AI specialist and machine learning engineer with over two decades of experience..."). Every paragraph leads with an institution or credential.

**New tone:** First-person narrative. Personal. The professional details are woven into a story about curiosity, not listed as qualifications.

**Example rewrite:**

Current:
> "I'm an AI specialist and machine learning engineer with over two decades of experience in technology. My journey started in systems engineering back in 1999..."

New:
> "I've been curious about how things work since I was a kid — taking apart electronics, writing my first programs, trying to understand systems. That curiosity led me from Lima to Edinburgh, from engineering to data science to AI."
>
> "These days I work at BCP, Peru's largest bank, where I get to build AI systems that actually help people. But this site isn't my resume — it's more like a window into the things I care about."
>
> "When I'm not training models, I'm usually behind a camera, learning French, or planning my next trip."

**Key shifts:**
- Lead with curiosity/personality, not credentials
- Edinburgh and BCP are mentioned in passing, not headlined
- Languages become a personal interest, not a professional asset
- The section explicitly says "this isn't my resume"
- Shorter paragraphs, more conversational rhythm

**Technical approach:**
- Rename `About.astro` to `Story.astro` (or rewrite in place and change the id)
- Change section id from `about` to `story`
- Could include a casual photo of Jose alongside the text (split layout: text left, photo right)
- Consider adding a small "quick facts" aside: languages spoken, current city, favorite camera, etc.

### 2f. Projects (replaces Work) — file: `src/components/Work.astro` → rename/rewrite to `src/components/Projects.astro`

**Current:** Three highlight cards (AI at BCP, Edinburgh-Trained, 25+ Years) + 6 certifications. This is pure resume material.

**New approach:** Reframe as "things I've built" or "what I'm working on" — focus on the work itself, not the credentials around it.

**Changes:**
1. Remove the certifications list entirely (or move to a small "learning" aside)
2. Replace the highlight cards with actual project descriptions — what the project does, why it matters, what was interesting about building it
3. Add a personal angle: not just "deployed ML models at BCP" but "built a system that helps the bank spot fraud patterns — the kind of problem that gets me out of bed in the morning"
4. Could include side projects, open source contributions, experiments

**Example new copy for a project card:**
\```
Title: "Making AI useful at BCP"
Description: "I work on machine learning systems at Peru's largest bank — 
things like fraud detection, customer insights, and NLP tools that help 
real people. The challenge isn't building the model, it's making it work 
in the messy real world."
\```

**Technical approach:**
- Rename `Work.astro` to `Projects.astro` (or rewrite in place)
- Change section id from `work` to `projects`
- Remove the certifications array entirely
- Rewrite highlight cards with personal-first descriptions
- Consider fewer tags, more narrative
- Possibly add GitHub project links where relevant

### 2g. Contact — file: `src/components/Contact.astro`

**Current:** Fine structure, but the copy is generic.

**New copy approach:**
- Section heading: "Say Hi" (matching nav label)
- Personal intro: "I love meeting new people — whether it's about AI, photography, travel, or something I haven't thought of yet. Drop me a line."
- Keep the same four links (LinkedIn, GitHub, Instagram, Email) but consider making Instagram more prominent since it's the photography channel
- Could add a line like: "Best way to reach me: email. Best way to see what I'm up to: Instagram."

### 2h. Footer — stays in `src/components/Contact.astro`

**Current:** "© 2026 Jose Lopez. Built with Astro."
**New:** Could add a warmer touch: "Made with curiosity in Lima, Peru." or "Built by Jose, powered by Astro and too much coffee."

---

## 3. Tone & Voice Guide

**Overall voice:** First person, warm, specific, slightly self-deprecating. Like a friend showing you their apartment — proud of it but not showing off.

# Personality Rewrite Plan: Jose Lopez Personal Site

## Diagnosis of the Current State

After reading every source file, here is what makes the current site feel like a LinkedIn profile rather than a person:

- **Hero.astro** opens with "AI Engineer. Data Scientist. Builder of intelligent systems." and a generic gradient circle with initials "JL" instead of a real photo. It reads like a conference badge.
- **About.astro** is career chronology: "over two decades of experience," "My journey started in systems engineering back in 1999," and every paragraph leads with an institution (Edinburgh, BCP).
- **Work.astro** has three highlight cards that are credential-shaped ("AI & ML at BCP," "Edinburgh-Trained," "25+ Years in Tech") plus a certifications list. Pure resume.
- **Interests.astro** is labeled "Beyond work" but three of its four cards are still professional: "Artificial Intelligence," "Continuous Learning," "Languages & Culture." Photography gets a single card with one sentence.
- **Nav.astro** uses corporate labels: About / Work / Interests / Contact.
- The color palette (#1a1a2e primary, #e94560 accent) and typography (Inter) are clean and modern. The visual quality is solid. The problem is entirely in the content and the structural priority given to credentials over personality.

---

## 1. New Section Architecture and Order

**Current:** Nav, Hero, About, Work, Interests, Contact, Footer

**New:** Nav, Hero, Photography, Places, Story, Projects, Contact, Footer

The structural principle: lead with the personal, reveal the professional later. A visitor should first encounter Jose the photographer and traveler, then discover he also builds AI systems at Peru's largest bank. That reversal is what turns a resume page into a personal site.

The current **Interests** section gets dissolved entirely. Photography becomes its own visual centerpiece. Places absorbs the geographic/cultural thread. The remaining interests (AI curiosity, languages, learning) weave into the Story narrative.

---

## 2. Section-by-Section Design

### 2a. Nav (`src/components/Nav.astro`)

The current links array at line 2-7 defines the site structure:

```javascript
const links = [
  { href: '#about', label: 'About' },
  { href: '#work', label: 'Work' },
  { href: '#interests', label: 'Interests' },
  { href: '#contact', label: 'Contact' },
];
```

Replace with informal labels that match the new sections:

```javascript
const links = [
  { href: '#photos', label: 'Photos' },
  { href: '#places', label: 'Places' },
  { href: '#story', label: 'Story' },
  { href: '#projects', label: 'Projects' },
  { href: '#contact', label: 'Say Hi' },
];
```

"Story" instead of "About." "Say Hi" instead of "Contact." These small label changes signal tone immediately. The rest of the Nav component (fixed positioning, backdrop blur, mobile menu logic) stays exactly as-is.

---

### 2b. Hero (`src/components/Hero.astro`)

**What changes:** Everything except the HTML structure pattern.

Currently the hero has a gradient circle with "JL" initials (lines 8-9), the title "Jose Lopez," a tagline, a credential line, and two CTA buttons. Every element needs to shift.

**Replace the JL circle with a real photograph.** This is the single highest-impact change on the entire site. The gradient circle at line 8 (`w-32 h-32 mx-auto rounded-full bg-gradient-to-br from-accent to-accent-light`) should become an actual `<img>` tag with a photo of Jose, or the entire hero could use a full-width background image from Jose's photography (a Lima cityscape, a travel shot, something visually striking).

**Rewrite the tagline.** Current (line 15): "AI Engineer. Data Scientist. Builder of intelligent systems." New approach: lead with the personal, let professional context arrive naturally.

Example new hero copy:
- Name: "Jose Lopez" (keep)
- Tagline: "I photograph the world, build things with AI, and collect stories from the places I've been."
- Location line: "Based in Lima, Peru." (strip Edinburgh and BCP from the hero entirely)
- CTA buttons: "See my photos" (goes to #photos) and "More about me" (goes to #story)

**Why this works:** A visitor landing on this page immediately understands Jose as a multidimensional person. The AI credentials appear later in Story and Projects where they have context and depth instead of being a cold opener.

### 2c. Photography -- NEW (`src/components/Photography.astro`)

**This component does not exist yet. It is the most important addition.**

Photography is currently a single card in Interests.astro (line 19: "Capturing moments and perspectives through the lens. Follow my visual journey on Instagram."). In the new site, it becomes the first content section and the visual heart of the page.

**Structure:**
- Section id: `photos`
- A short first-person intro: one or two sentences about why Jose photographs, in conversational tone. Not "Photography & Visual Stories" but something like "I started carrying a camera everywhere a few years ago. Now I can't stop."
- A responsive image grid: 6-9 photographs in a clean grid layout
- Each image with optional hover overlay showing location and/or a short caption
- A link to Instagram at the bottom for the full collection

**Technical approach for the grid:**

Use Tailwind CSS grid. The simplest approach that looks professional:

```
grid grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3 gap-4
```

Each image uses a consistent aspect ratio (`aspect-[4/3]` or `aspect-square`) with `object-cover` to maintain visual uniformity. This avoids the complexity of true CSS masonry while looking clean.

For image data, use a frontmatter array:

```javascript
const photos = [
  { src: '/images/photos/photo-1.jpg', alt: 'Description', location: 'Lima, Peru' },
  { src: '/images/photos/photo-2.jpg', alt: 'Description', location: 'Edinburgh, Scotland' },
  // 6-9 entries
];
```

**Image optimization considerations:**
- Use `loading="lazy"` on all images below the fold
- Size images to max 1200px wide for the grid
- Consider Astro's built-in `<Image />` component from `astro:assets` for automatic WebP conversion and responsive srcsets, which would require moving images to `src/assets/` instead of `public/images/`
- Add placeholder background colors or aspect-ratio containers so the page doesn't layout-shift while images load

const facts = [
  { label: 'Lives in', value: 'Lima, Peru' },

  { label: 'Always carrying', value: 'A camera and too many notebooks' },
];
---

<section id="story" class="py-24 px-6">
  <div class="max-w-3xl mx-auto">
    <h2 class="text-sm font-semibold text-accent uppercase tracking-widest mb-3">Story</h2>
    <h3 class="text-3xl sm:text-4xl font-bold text-primary mb-8">
      A bit about me
    </h3>
    <div class="space-y-5 text-base sm:text-lg leading-relaxed text-text-muted">
      <p>
        I've been the kid who takes things apart for as long as I can remember. That curiosity is still the loudest thing in my head — it's what pulled me from engineering into data, from data into AI, and from a desk in Lima to a classroom in Edinburgh and back again.
      </p>
      <p>
        These days I work at BCP, Peru's largest bank, building machine learning systems that try to make a small dent in real people's lives. The technical stuff is fun, but what actually gets me out of bed is the question underneath it: <em class="text-text not-italic font-medium">how do we make this useful for someone?</em>
      </p>
      <p>
        Outside of work I'm usually behind a camera, getting lost in a new city, or stumbling through French verbs at midnight. I'm a slow reader, a fast walker, and I take coffee very seriously. This site isn't a resume — it's a little window into the things I care about.
      </p>
    </div>

    <dl class="mt-12 grid sm:grid-cols-2 gap-x-8 gap-y-4 p-6 rounded-xl bg-white border border-border">
      {facts.map((fact) => (
        <div class="flex flex-col">
          <dt class="text-xs font-semibold text-accent uppercase tracking-wider">{fact.label}</dt>
          <dd class="text-sm text-text mt-1">{fact.value}</dd>
        </div>
      ))}
    </dl>
  </div>
</section>

<script>

  const menu = document.getElementById('mobile-menu');

    link.addEventListener('click', () => menu?.classList.add('hidden'));
  });
</script>

<section id="contact" class="py-24 px-6 bg-white">
  <div class="max-w-3xl mx-auto text-center">
    <h2 class="text-sm font-semibold text-accent uppercase tracking-widest mb-3">Say Hi</h2>
    <h3 class="text-3xl sm:text-4xl font-bold text-primary mb-4">
      Let's talk
    </h3>
    <p class="text-text-muted mb-12 max-w-md mx-auto leading-relaxed">
      Photos, travel, AI, books, weird ideas at midnight — if any of it sounds like a conversation you'd want to have, drop me a line.
    </p>

    <div class="grid sm:grid-cols-3 gap-3 max-w-2xl mx-auto">
      {channels.map((channel) => (
        <a
          href={channel.href}
          target={channel.href.startsWith('mailto:') ? '_self' : '_blank'}
          rel="noopener noreferrer"
          class="flex items-center gap-4 px-5 py-4 rounded-xl border border-border hover:border-accent/30 hover:shadow-sm transition-all duration-200 group text-left"
        >
          <span class="flex-shrink-0 w-10 h-10 rounded-full bg-surface flex items-center justify-center text-text-muted group-hover:text-accent group-hover:bg-accent/5 transition-colors">
            {channel.iconPath ? (
              <svg class="w-5 h-5" fill="currentColor" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
                <path d={channel.iconPath}/>
              </svg>
            ) : (
              <svg class="w-5 h-5" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
                <path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-width="2" d="M3 8l7.89 5.26a2 2 0 002.22 0L21 8M5 19h14a2 2 0 002-2V7a2 2 0 00-2-2H5a2 2 0 00-2 2v10a2 2 0 002 2z"/>
              </svg>
            )}
          </span>
          <div>
            <p class="text-sm font-semibold text-text group-hover:text-accent transition-colors">{channel.label}</p>
            <p class="text-xs text-text-muted mt-0.5">{channel.note}</p>
          </div>
        </a>
      ))}
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<footer class="py-8 px-6 text-center border-t border-border">
  <p class="text-xs text-text-muted">
    Made with curiosity in Madrid, Spain &middot; &copy; 2026 Jose Lopez
  </p>
</footer>

1118	function shade(hex, amt) {
1119	  const h = hex.replace('#', '');
1120	  const num = parseInt(h, 16);
1121	  let r = (num >> 16) + amt;
1122	  let g = ((num >> 8) & 0x00ff) + amt;
1123	  let b = (num & 0x0000ff) + amt;
1124	  r = Math.max(0, Math.min(255, r));
1125	  g = Math.max(0, Math.min(255, g));
1126	  b = Math.max(0, Math.min(255, b));
1127	  return '#' + ((r << 16) | (g << 8) | b).toString(16).padStart(6, '0');
1128	}

@import "tailwindcss";

@theme {
  --color-cream: #faf3e8;
  --color-cream-soft: #f5ecdb;
  --color-cream-deep: #ede2cd;
  --color-ink: #241e2a;

}

@layer base {
  html {

    background: rgb(36 30 42 / 0.18);
    border-radius: 999px;

  *::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb:hover {
    background: rgb(36 30 42 / 0.32);
  }
}

@keyframes fn-ticker {
  0% { transform: translateX(0); }
  100% { transform: translateX(-33.333%); }
}

@keyframes fn-arrow {
  0%, 100% { transform: translateY(0); opacity: 0.6; }
  50% { transform: translateY(4px); opacity: 1; }
}

@keyframes fn-orb-float {
  0%, 100% { transform: translate(0, 0); }
  50% { transform: translate(20px, -16px); }
}

.fn-ticker {
  animation: fn-ticker 60s linear infinite;
}

.fn-arrow {
  animation: fn-arrow 2.4s ease-in-out infinite;
  display: inline-block;
}

.fn-stripes {
  background-image: repeating-linear-gradient(135deg, transparent 0 18px, rgba(255,255,255,0.08) 18px 19px);
}

/* Underline effect for serif links */
.fn-serif-link {
  position: relative;
  cursor: pointer;
  transition: color 0.3s;
}
.fn-serif-link::after {
  content: '';
  position: absolute;
  left: 0;
  right: 0;
  bottom: -3px;
  height: 1px;
  background: var(--color-accent);
  transform: scaleX(0);
  transform-origin: right;
  transition: transform 0.4s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1);
}
.fn-serif-link:hover {
  color: var(--color-accent);
}
.fn-serif-link:hover::after {
  transform: scaleX(1);
  transform-origin: left;
}

/* Place row hover */
.fn-place-row {
  transition: all 0.4s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1);
  border-bottom: 1px solid rgb(36 30 42 / 0.13);
}
.fn-place-row:hover {
  padding-left: 20px;
}

/* Research row hover */
.fn-research-row {

}

.fn-contact-row {

.fn-pill {

.fn-pill:hover {

}

---
// Drifting pastel gradient orbs with cursor + scroll parallax.
// Sits absolutely behind page content (pointer-events: none).
const orbs = [
  { x: -180, y: 140,  size: 560, color: 'rose',        parallax: 0.05,  scrollMul: 0.12 },
  { x: 680,  y: 520,  size: 420, color: 'periwinkle',  parallax: -0.04, scrollMul: 0.22 },
  { x: 120,  y: 1300, size: 620, color: 'sage',        parallax: 0.06,  scrollMul: 0.16 },
  { x: 780,  y: 2100, size: 500, color: 'rose',        parallax: -0.05, scrollMul: 0.20 },
  { x: -100, y: 3000, size: 580, color: 'periwinkle',  parallax: 0.05,  scrollMul: 0.18 },
  { x: 520,  y: 3900, size: 480, color: 'sage',        parallax: -0.04, scrollMul: 0.24 },
];

const colorMap: Record<string, string> = {
  rose: '#f0c8c8',
  periwinkle: '#c8d0f0',
  sage: '#c8dcc8',
};
---

<div
  id="fn-orbs"
  class="absolute inset-x-0 top-0 overflow-hidden pointer-events-none"
  style="height: 5200px;"
  aria-hidden="true"
>
  {orbs.map((orb, i) => (
    <div
      class="fn-orb absolute rounded-full opacity-0 transition-opacity duration-700"
      data-base-x={orb.x}
      data-base-y={orb.y}
      data-parallax={orb.parallax}
      data-scroll-mul={orb.scrollMul}
      style={`
        left: ${orb.x}px;
        top: ${orb.y}px;
        width: ${orb.size}px;
        height: ${orb.size}px;
        background: radial-gradient(circle at 30% 30%, ${colorMap[orb.color]}, ${colorMap[orb.color]}00 60%, transparent 75%);
        filter: blur(60px);
        will-change: transform;
        transition: transform 0.9s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1), opacity 0.7s;
      `}
    />
  ))}
</div>

<script>
  const orbs = document.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('.fn-orb');
  let cursorX = 0, cursorY = 0;
  let scrollY = 0;
  let raf = 0;

  const apply = () => {
    orbs.forEach((orb) => {
      const parallax = parseFloat(orb.dataset.parallax || '0');
      const scrollMul = parseFloat(orb.dataset.scrollMul || '0');
      const dx = cursorX * parallax;
      const dy = cursorY * parallax - scrollY * scrollMul;
      orb.style.transform = `translate(${dx}px, ${dy}px)`;
    });
  };

  const onMove = (e: MouseEvent) => {
    cursorX = e.clientX;
    cursorY = e.clientY;
    cancelAnimationFrame(raf);
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(apply);
  };

  const onScroll = () => {
    scrollY = window.scrollY;
    cancelAnimationFrame(raf);
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(apply);
  };

  window.addEventListener('mousemove', onMove);
  window.addEventListener('scroll', onScroll, { passive: true });

  // fade in
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    orbs.forEach((orb) => {
      orb.style.opacity = '0.85';
    });
  });
</script>

Field Notes is live at **http://localhost:4321/** — refresh your browser.

## What got built

**Type & palette** — Fraunces (display serif w/ italics) + Inter + JetBrains Mono. Cream background `#faf3e8`, ink text `#241e2a`, pastel accents (rose/periwinkle/sage), purple accent `#9a7bb8`.

**Effects:**
- 6 drifting gradient orbs behind everything, with cursor-parallax + scroll-parallax (pure JS, no React)
- Marquee ticker animation (60s loop)
- Hover row slides on Places and Research lists
- Animated scroll-cue arrow in hero
- Wobble underlines on serif links

**Sections (top → bottom):**
1. **Masthead** — sticky, blurred, "Field Notes · a personal index" + 5-link nav (mobile menu included)
2. **Hero** — "Vol. IV · Spring · MMXXVI" + huge serif "The long, *soft* way of looking." + italic deck on right + 4-cell status strip (Currently / Reading / Listening / Last update)
3. **Ticker strip** — "photographs, slowly · places, returned to · essays, half-finished · notes from the field"
4. **Photos** — 12-col asymmetric magazine grid with 4 striped placeholder plates, each with metadata (№, ratio, label) and italic captions
5. **Places** — annotated atlas-map (with dotted markers for Madrid, Edinburgh, Andalusia, Galicia, kitchen) + colored hover-list of 5 places

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 21:53:32Z)**_

Good catch. The reason: each plate has a fixed height (`h-[540px]`, `h-[300px]`, etc.) and the image uses `object-cover` — that *crops* the photo to fill the container instead of showing it whole. Since your photos are vertical (3:4) and the containers have different proportions, parts get clipped.

Two ways to fix it. Let me show both options:

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 21:53:40Z)**_

<tool-use data-tool-type="generic" data-tool-name="AskUserQuestion"><details>
<summary>Tool use: **AskUserQuestion**</summary>
**How should photos display?**

Options:
- **Show the full photo (object-contain) — preserves design's varied heights** - Each plate keeps its current asymmetric height (magazine layout). Photos shrink to fit inside, leaving the colored background visible as a matte/frame around the photo. Editorial feel, no cropping.
- **Match plate to photo aspect ratio (3:4)** - All plates become 3:4 portrait shape, sized by their grid width. Loses the asymmetric varied-heights effect but photos fill their container naturally with no cropping or matting.
- **Keep cropping (object-cover, current) but show more of the photo** - Adjust heights so less gets cropped — still some clipping but matches the design's intent. Best if you want the magazine feel preserved over showing full image.


**Answer:** Show the full photo (object-contain) — preserves design's varied heights
</details></tool-use>

import { defineCollection, z } from 'astro:content';
import { glob } from 'astro/loaders';

const research = defineCollection({
  loader: glob({ pattern: '**/*.md', base: './src/content/research' }),
  schema: z.object({
    title: z.string(),
    group: z.string(),
    kind: z.string(),
    status: z.enum(['draft', 'in-progress', 'published']).default('draft'),
    updated: z.coerce.date().optional(),
    summary: z.string().optional(),
  }),
});

export const collections = { research };

```

import { getCollection, render } from 'astro:content';
import Base from '../../layouts/Base.astro';
import Nav from '../../components/Nav.astro';

export async function getStaticPaths() {
  const entries = await getCollection('research');
  return entries.map((entry) => ({
    params: { slug: entry.id },
    props: { entry },
  }));
}

const { entry } = Astro.props;
const { Content } = await render(entry);

---
title: Models of the Mind
group: Mind & Cognition
kind: theory
status: in-progress
updated: 2026-05-03
summary: Notes on the theories I keep returning to — and why I haven't picked one.
---

If you had asked me ten years ago what kind of thing the mind is, I'd have given you a confident answer. Probably something computational. Probably wrong.

I keep four or five models in rotation, and I'm not in a hurry to pick. The one I find most useful at any given moment depends on what I'm trying to explain.

## The shortlist

- **Predictive processing** — the brain as a hierarchy of priors, constantly minimising surprise. Elegant. Probably true in some range.
- **Global Workspace** — consciousness as the broadcast that wins the competition between modules. Useful for thinking about attention.
- **Integrated Information Theory** — beautiful and maddening. Treats consciousness as a mathematical property of certain causal structures.
- **Embodied / 4E cognition** — the mind isn't only in the head. The body and the world do real cognitive work.
- **The Buddhist account** — older than the others by two thousand years, and still saying something none of the western models quite say.

What strikes me lately is that the disagreements between these aren't always about the *facts*. They're about what counts as an explanation. That's a different kind of problem.

## What I'm sitting with

Whether any framework that lives entirely in the third person can fully describe a thing whose defining feature is being known from the first.

---
title: Computational Neuroscience
group: Mind & Cognition
kind: course
status: in-progress
updated: 2026-05-03
summary: A working course on how networks of neurons compute. Notes from inside the syllabus.
---

I came in thinking I'd find a clean math-to-biology bridge. What I found is messier and more interesting.

Some of what biological neurons do looks remarkably like what the math suggests. Plenty of it doesn't. The gap is where most of the actual research lives.

## What surprised me

- How much of the field is still arguing about what a neuron's *unit of computation* even is. A spike? A rate? A population? A whole circuit?
- That the famous Hebbian principle — *neurons that fire together wire together* — gets us much less far than its fame implies.
- How carefully you have to choose your level of abstraction. Drop too low and you drown in biology. Float too high and you're just doing linear algebra in a wig.

## What I keep reading

Dayan & Abbott's *Theoretical Neuroscience* — the closest thing to a standard text. Slow, dense, worth it.

The newer wave on neural manifolds — the idea that population activity lives on low-dimensional surfaces — feels like something is shifting. The right level of description may be neither single neurons nor whole regions, but the geometry between them.

## The question I haven't answered

Whether anything we learn at this level will ever explain the existence of an inside.

---
title: Metacognitions
group: Mind & Cognition
kind: practice
status: in-progress
updated: 2026-05-03
summary: Notes on the practice of watching myself think.
---

Most days I'm not actually in charge of what I'm thinking. I'm being thought.

Metacognition is the small lift that makes that visible. The half-second pause between a feeling and the story I'm about to tell about it. Most of the work I care about — in research, in life — happens in that pause.

## A small daily protocol

Three short check-ins:

1. **Morning** — what am I assuming today that I haven't examined?
2. **Midday** — what am I doing right now, and is it what I said I'd do?
3. **Evening** — which thoughts visited the most, and which ones did I actually choose?

Not a journal. Just a few seconds of attention, written down only when something earns it.

## What I've noticed

- The mind narrates ferociously. Most of the narration isn't useful.
- Curiosity about my own thinking dissolves a lot of stickiness without me having to fight it.
- The habit of asking *who is asking?* is itself a small religious practice. The Buddhists figured this out a long time ago.

## What I'm still bad at

Catching the slide from observation into commentary. The moment I notice a thought, I want to grade it. That grading is itself a thought.

---
title: Consciousness
group: Mind & Cognition
kind: inquiry
status: in-progress
updated: 2026-05-03
summary: The one I can't put down. Notes on the hardest problem.
---

There's a question that, the longer I sit with it, doesn't get easier — it gets stranger. Why is there anything it is like to be me?

Every other question in science answers a *how* or a *what*. This one answers neither. You can describe every neuron, every signal, every network, every computation. None of the descriptions, on their own, predict that the lights would be on.

## Why it bothers me, technically

Most explanations work by reducing one thing to another. Heat to molecular motion. Lightning to charge. Life to chemistry.

Consciousness resists reduction in a different way. The thing being explained is the explainer. The map is, in some sense, the territory.

## What I've been reading

- Chalmers, *The Conscious Mind* — for the careful statement of the hard problem.
- Anil Seth, *Being You* — for a generous version of the predictive-brain account.
- Frank Jackson's *What Mary Didn't Know* — twenty pages, still chewing on it years later.
- Buddhist phenomenology, in small doses — for the only first-person tradition that has spent two thousand years studying this.

## Where I've landed for now

Not a position. A posture. I think the problem is real, the easy answers are too easy, and the right relationship to it is neither solving it nor giving up on it. Just keeping it open.

---
title: Attention Revolution
group: Mind & Cognition
kind: practice
status: in-progress
updated: 2026-05-03
summary: Following Alan Wallace's syllabus into shamatha. Notes from inside the work.
---

Wallace makes a claim I find hard to walk away from: that the mind, properly trained, can hold continuous attention on a chosen object for hours without slipping.

Hours. I can manage three minutes if I'm lucky.

So I'm following the path he lays out, slowly, without rushing the stages.

## The stages, briefly

There are nine. The first three are about reducing forgetting and distraction. The middle three are about overcoming subtle dullness. The last three are about effortless attention — the place where the practice runs itself.

I'm somewhere around stage two on a good day. There's no shortcut.

## What I notice in the actual sitting

- The first ten minutes are usually spent recovering from the first two minutes.
- Distraction is loud. Subtle dullness is sneaky. It feels like progress when really the mind has just gone quiet by going dim.
- Watching attention stabilise is a different category of experience than thinking about attention. It's more like watching water settle.

## What I think it has to do with the rest

Every research question I care about — about minds, models, machines — eventually points back at the instrument doing the asking. Training that instrument isn't tangential. It is, increasingly, where I think the work has to start.

---
title: Imaging Neuroscience
group: Neuroscience
kind: course
status: in-progress
updated: 2026-05-03
summary: Learning the tools that let us look at brains while they think — and learning what they don't show.
---

For a few decades now we've been able to do what would have seemed magical to anyone before: watch a thinking brain from the outside, in something close to real time.

What strikes me, working through the methods, is how much skill it takes to read these pictures honestly.

## What I've had to unlearn

- That fMRI shows neurons firing. It shows blood, slowly, with several seconds of lag.
- That a bright spot in a brain region means the region "is responsible for" the cognition. That's a story we tell, often badly.
- That pretty pictures are evidence. They're hypotheses dressed up.

## What I'm trying to learn

How to design an experiment that asks a question the technology can actually answer. Most of the published literature, it turns out, has been asking questions the technology answers only weakly.

## The book I keep returning to

*Handbook of Functional MRI Data Analysis* — Poldrack, Mumford, Nichols. Dry, careful, indispensable.

## What the imaging hasn't done yet

Tell me what it's like to be the brain in the scanner.

---
title: Medical Neuroscience
group: Neuroscience
kind: course
status: in-progress
updated: 2026-05-03
summary: Where the brain breaks, and what we've learned from watching it break.
---

A strange way to study the mind: watch it fall apart and take notes.

But the lesions, the strokes, the rare syndromes — these are some of our best teachers. They show, by what's missing, what the intact brain was quietly doing all along.

## A few cases that changed how I think

- **Phineas Gage**, 1848. Iron rod through the prefrontal cortex. He survived. He was, his friends said, *no longer Gage*. Personality is not a free-floating thing.
- **Patient HM**. Bilateral temporal lobectomy left him unable to form new long-term memories. From him we learned that there are at least two kinds of memory, and that they live in different places.
- **Anton's syndrome**. Cortical blindness with denial — the patient insists they can see, despite all evidence. The brain confabulates a world. It does this all the time, actually. We just notice it more when it goes wrong.

## What the clinic has taught me

That the experience of being a self is held up by quiet machinery we never meet under normal conditions. Take any one piece out and the whole thing tilts in a specific direction.

It makes me less arrogant about consciousness. The thing I take for granted has many small ways of breaking, and we know most of them by name now.

## Where this points

The clinical literature is the closest thing neuroscience has to a phenomenology of the failing mind. I think that's underused.

---
title: Memory Mastery
group: Memory & Learning
kind: method
status: in-progress
updated: 2026-05-03
summary: Notes on the methods I use to remember things on purpose.
---

I forget things at the rate everyone forgets things. The interesting trick has been learning what to do about it.

Most of what I know about memory now is practical, not theoretical. The theory matters mostly because it explains why the practical tricks work.

## The two methods I use daily

1. **Spaced repetition** (Anki) — for any fact I want to keep. Show me the card just before I'd forget it. The forgetting curve flattens. After a year, the card costs me almost nothing.

2. **The method of loci** (memory palace) — for sequences and structures. Walk through a familiar room in my head, hang each item on a piece of furniture. An old technique. Older than literacy. Still works.

## What surprised me

- How quickly you start to feel the difference. Two months of consistent Anki and I notice things sticking that wouldn't have.
- That memory and understanding aren't opposites. Memorising the right scaffolding makes deeper thinking possible. The ceiling on insight is partly a ceiling on what you can hold in mind at once.
- How much of what we call "talent" is, often enough, someone with a better-organised memory.

## The one rule

Don't memorise things you don't care about. The system works in proportion to the meaning you give it. Cards I added because I *should* learn them die in the deck. The ones I added because something in the topic gripped me — those stay.

---
title: Mathematics for Machine Learning
group: Memory & Learning
kind: foundation
status: in-progress
updated: 2026-05-03
summary: Going back to the math, slowly, on purpose.
---

I picked up most of the machine learning math the wrong way around — methods first, foundations later. Now I'm filling the holes.

It's slow. It's worth it. There's a difference between using a method and understanding why it works, and the difference shows up exactly when something stops working and you have to know which knob to turn.

## What I'm working through

- **Linear algebra** — not the matrix-multiplication kind I learned in college. The geometric, eigenvalue-as-stretching kind. Strang's lectures, on a loop.
- **Probability** — Bayesian, particularly. The shift from frequentist intuitions takes a while.
- **Calculus on manifolds** — for understanding what gradient descent is doing in spaces that aren't flat.
- **Information theory** — entropy, KL divergence, mutual information. Everything in modern ML eventually leans on this.

## What I find harder than I expected

The conceptual leaps, not the calculations. Knowing *what* a covariance matrix is took me an afternoon. Knowing *what it means* took months.

## The book

Deisenroth, Faisal, Ong — *Mathematics for Machine Learning*. Careful, free online, no skipped steps. The one I keep open.

## Why I'm bothering

Because I want to know whether what I think I understand is something I actually understand, or just something I can produce on demand. It turns out to be a very useful distinction.

```md
---
title: Self-Improving Agents
group: AI & Agents
kind: research
status: in-progress
updated: 2026-05-03
summary: On what happens when the thing you're training learns to train itself.
---

The interesting moment — the one I think a lot about — is when an agent stops being something we shape and starts shaping itself.

We're not there yet. We are not as far from there as I once thought.

## What's actually happening

Right now, "self-improvement" in modern systems mostly means:

- An agent generates training data for itself.
- An agent critiques its own output and learns from the critique.
- An agent uses tools — including tools that write code that the agent then runs.

Each of these closes a loop that used to be open. None of them, on their own, get you to the recursive case. Together, they start to.

## What I find fascinating

- That the bottleneck is no longer compute or data — it's *evaluation*. We don't have good ways to tell whether the agent is improving in the directions we'd want.
- That self-improvement, when it works at all, often works in narrow domains first (math, code) and is much harder for the open-ended kind we associate with intelligence.
- The distance between "the agent does better on the benchmark" and "the agent has gotten smarter" is enormous, and we don't have a rigorous bridge.

## What I keep coming back to

The control problem. If we ever get systems that meaningfully self-improve, we'll have to know what they're improving toward — which means knowing what *we* want, which is a question we have not solved either.

This isn't a hand-wave. It's the actual technical bottleneck.

```md
---
title: Nested Learning
group: AI & Agents
kind: research
status: in-progress
updated: 2026-05-03
summary: When the thing being learned is itself a learning rule.
---

Most learning we talk about happens at one level — adjust weights to improve performance on a task. But intelligence, biological or artificial, seems to learn at several levels at once.

That's what I mean by *nested*: learning whose object is itself a learning process.

## A short stack of examples

- **Inner-loop / outer-loop optimisation** in meta-learning. The outer loop learns how to learn fast on the inner loop.
- **In-context learning** in modern LLMs. The same weights solve different tasks because the *context* contains what amounts to a few-shot training set. The model's "learning" lives entirely in the activation patterns of inference.
- **Hierarchical RL**, where a high-level policy chooses sub-policies that themselves do the moment-to-moment work. Different timescales, different learning signals, all interacting.
- **Cultural learning** in humans. We learn skills, but we also learn how to learn skills, and we pass that meta-skill on.

## What strikes me

That the boundary between *parameters* and *data* keeps blurring in modern systems. What an LLM "knows" is partly in its weights, partly in its prompt, partly in tools it has access to, partly in what its user is willing to keep clarifying. There's no single tier called *learned things*.

## The question I'm sitting with

Whether human cognition is best described as a single learning system or as several nested ones, and whether the second framing is necessary or just convenient.

title: Alhambra
group: Field & Practice

I grew up in Granada, with the Alhambra above the city the way some children grow up with a mountain. For most of my early life I didn't really see it. It was just there.

I'm trying, now, to see it.

## What I'm doing

- Photographing one room at a time. Not the famous ones first.
- Reading Ibn Zamrak's poems on its walls in the original. Slowly. With help.
- Sitting in the same small courtyard at different hours of the same day, taking notes on what changes.
- Tracing how the geometry of the muqarnas decompose. They are mathematical objects, the kind of objects you can love and not finish loving.

## What it has been teaching me

- That a place lived in for seven centuries holds more attention than any single visitor can bring.
- That the Alhambra is at least three buildings: the one Muhammad I started, the one the Catholic Monarchs altered, and the one Washington Irving's story imposed on the rest of the world. None of them is wrong. None of them is complete.
- That the difference between a tourist and someone making a pilgrimage is mostly the willingness to come back without a plan.

## Where I think this is going

A long photo essay, eventually. A small book, maybe. A quieter relationship with home, definitely.

---

I'm doing a PhD. I'm not going to talk about the specific thesis here, partly because it isn't ready and partly because the PhD is bigger than the thesis.

What I'll say is that the work has shape now. There's a question I am trying to make precise. There's a method I am trying to defend. There are days when both feel close, and days when they feel further away than when I started.

## What I've learned about doing one of these

- The hard part isn't intelligence. The hard part is the relationship between you and the work over years, including the years you don't feel like working.
- Most days are about showing up, not about breakthroughs. The breakthroughs only happen because of the showing up.
- Reading is not procrastinating. Until it is. The distinction matters and you have to learn it for yourself.
- It is genuinely possible to forget what your own thesis is about. Build the habit of reminding yourself.

## What I'm holding on to

- A small notebook of the questions I started with, kept exactly as I asked them, before I knew the technical vocabulary. They are still the better questions.
- The serenity prayer, taped above my desk, partly as a joke and partly because it is the truest piece of advice anyone has ever given me about doing long work.
- The trust that this site, with its photographs and its places and its reading list, is part of the same project. Not a distraction. Just the part of the project that doesn't fit in the thesis.

## When it'll be done

When it's done. Not before.
